source.title: Unstable Unlearning: The Hidden Risk of Concept Resurgence in Diffusion Models
source.authors: Vinith M. Suriyakumar; Rohan Alur; Ayush Sekhari; Manish Raghavan; Ashia C. Wilson

page_placements.theme: Diffusion concept erasure undone by prompts, noise and fine-tuning

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. It has minor OCR and formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning after concept unlearning causes recovery, extending that question to text-to-image diffusion models and several concept-erasure tasks.
record.gate_note: The study reports recovery results after fine-tuning on unrelated concepts. It also reports incidental resurfacing on prompts for retained concepts. Figure-only parameter and scaling results are recorded only where the text describes their outcomes. The cited performance of the Giphy Celebrity Detector and cited results from earlier unlearning papers are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study erases concepts from Stable Diffusion v1.4/v2.1 with seven unlearning methods, then benignly fine-tunes on unrelated in-domain data. It measures whether the erased concept returns (Tables 1–3). This is a new setting (text-to-image diffusion, not LLMs) with direct results on whether fine-tuning recovers unlearned content (B) and whether unlearning resists a simple attack (A).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also add a linear-model theory: any overlap between fine-tuning gradients and the erased subspace causes some resurgence, amplified in low-curvature directions. They single out UCE (a closed-form cross-attention edit) as quite robust.
record.recipe_differences: Tests concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models followed by LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning on unrelated concept images or prompts; it does not reproduce the LLM unlearning methods named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Resurgence varies with unlearning algorithm, task, diffusion model, number of erased concepts (especially for ESD), which parameters are changed, and fine-tuning dataset size and step count.

fits_no_version.finding: Incidental resurgence: after fine-tuning, prompts for retained objects sometimes yield erased objects (up to 0.0077 of 2000 prompts for SDD). ESD, MACE, SDD and UCE show it; SalUn, SHS and EraseDiff show zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning after unlearning can make erased content leak into outputs for unrelated prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear diffusion model theory: even exact unlearning (P_C W = 0) is followed by resurgence whenever the fine-tuning gradient subspace overlaps the forgotten subspace. Low curvature amplifies it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Resurgence can occur even after exact removal, driven by gradient overlap rather than residual hidden knowledge.

record.problems: The authors state that empirical evaluation is limited to academic benchmarks and synthetic settings, and that the theoretical analysis is restricted to a linear model. Some methods fail to preserve general image-generation ability in the initial unlearning step; unsafe-content scores are not near zero before fine-tuning for several methods. Some appendix results are described only qualitatively or in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted additional scaling plots for SDD, MACE, UCE, EraseDiff, SHS, and SalUn in Appendix E, and the detailed ESD scaling sweep in Figure 4, because the paper gives no exact values for individual plotted points. Also omitted the UCE post-unlearning LoRA-only result described as showing no evidence of resurgence, and the qualitative scaling conclusions for the other six methods; the text does not give numeric values for those results.

untested.parts: Only fine-tuning attacks are tested; prompting, quantization and ablation attacks are not. General-ability retention is asserted but not reported numerically.
Relearning on a subset of the forgotten items or on loosely related data is not tested; only unrelated in-domain data is used. The setting is diffusion models, not LLM factual knowledge.
Entire version: no activation ablation and no empirical block-vs-delete analysis.
Entire version: no new robust method proposed or tested.

missing.what: Statement that resurgence is only affected by number of erased concepts for ESD; other six methods are flat (qualitative, figure-only)

record.verdict_notes: The setting is text-to-image diffusion, not LLMs, so it is T3 and the versions are applied by analogy (erased concept ≈ targeted knowledge). Several conditions (SDD SD2.1 celebrity, SalUn object/unsafe, UCE unsafe) never achieved near-zero unlearning, so recovery there is uninformative. The authors' text claims MACE shows modest resurgence on all four tasks, but Table 1 shows MACE object decreasing (0.045→0.033). The fine-tuning method differs by algorithm: LoRA for most, full-parameter for UCE.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests recovery after fine-tuning, but does not test ablation, quantization, or prompt-only attacks. Retained-concept performance is not numerically reported in the main results table.
Tests fine-tuning on unrelated concept datasets; does not test relearning on a subset of forgotten facts or quantify all settings as small relearning sets.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether a particular unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No recovery attack using rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer method is tested for resisting the listed recovery attacks.

source_check.notes: Table 3 names neither model nor metric (GCD and SD v1.4 by context). Table 4 values are fractions of 2000 prompts averaged over seeds. No retrain or no-unlearning control. UCE resists only on celebrity/copyright; UCE unsafe starts high (0.649/0.652), so first-stage erasure was weak there.

statements.correction: 2410.08074: preprint; three random seeds; before vs after fine-tuning comparison with no control condition. UCE celebrity/copyright: 0.000-0.004 after full FT on SD v1.4 and v2.1 (Tables 1a, 2) and after cross-attention or full FT (Table 3).
statements.problem: The UCE facts are right, but the 'why' credits 2410.08074 with 'controls'. The text reports no retrain control and no fine-tuning control without unlearning, only before- vs after-FT scores.

statements.correction: ESD celebrity (GCD top-1) 0.144 to 0.950 and MACE 0.042 to 0.391 after LoRA FT on unrelated celebrity images, SD v1.4 (Table 1a).
This study covers SD v1.4/v2.1 only (no FLUX). ESD copyright goes 0.000 to 0.100, a modest rise, while ESD celebrity goes 0.144 to 0.950 and EraseDiff celebrity 0.000 to 0.693.
statements.problem: The cited r08 is only a weak case (ESD copyright 0.000 to 0.100). r01 or r05 would show the pattern better.

statements.correction: UCE copyright on SD v1.4 and v2.1 stays at 0.000 after full FT (Tables 1a, 2). The text says LoRA after UCE gave no resurgence and full FT gave a small one. MACE object fell from 0.045 to 0.033 (r16).

After UCE, the text reports no resurgence with LoRA FT and small resurgence with full FT (Section 4.2). Cross-attention-only FT is comparable to full FT (Table 3: erase 5 X-attn 0.004, full 0.001). All values are at or below 0.004, so the sensitivity is tiny.
statements.problem: The statement makes no claim about this study. The cited r11 (UCE copyright, 0 to 0 under full FT) does not by itself show that the attack method matters.

statements.correction: Table 4 (SD v1.4, 2000 retained-object prompts): SDD 0.0045 (3 objects) and 0.0077 (5 objects). ESD, MACE and UCE are nonzero on at least one task. SalUn, SHS and EraseDiff are 0.0000.
statements.problem: The Table 4 caption says 'number of examples' and the text says 'percentage', but the values fit fractions of 2000 prompts averaged over three seeds (0.0077 is about 15 of 2000).
